title: From atoms to aircraft: the future of flight demands a new approach to composites

Composite materials have already proven their worth in aerospace applications, from structural aircraft components to interior elements such as luggage compartments and passenger seatbacks.Credit: Jaromir Chalabala/ Shutterstock In 2030, if all goes well, Swiss explorer and environmentalist Bertrand Piccard plans to fly around the world, non-stop, in an aircraft powered by hydrogen fuel cells. The nine-day flight, known as Climate Impulse, intends to demonstrate the potential of hydrogen-powered aviation, but first the project must overcome a fundamental engineering constraint: mass. The aircraft must be light enough for the power supplied by its fuel cells, and the tanks of liquid hydrogen that fuel them, to carry it across oceans. To help achieve this, its designers have turned to Syensqo, a specialty materials company and technology partner of Climate Impulse, to supply adhesives and composite materials for the airframe and polymer membranes for the fuel cells. Composite materials typically comprise a thermosetting, thermoplastic or ceramic matrix and reinforcing fibres. By varying the chemistry of the resin matrix and the choice of reinforcing fibre, researchers can tailor these materials for a wide range of applications and environments. Five decades of innovation in the aerospace industry have demonstrated the utility of composite materials for applications including fuselages, wings and tail sections, as well as interior components such as luggage compartments and passenger seatbacks. Reducing the mass of Piccard’s aircraft by 600 kg could add more than 3,000 km of range. Composite materials are a natural choice as their favourable ratio of stiffness to density means a composite component can be 20-40% lighter than a comparable metal part while providing similar strength or stiffness. But Syensqo’s aerospace work extends beyond a single record-breaking flight. “Over the next several years, we’ll see demonstrations that will impact all of us,” says Stephen Heinz, vice president of composite materials research and innovation at Syensqo. One example is the emerging generation of aircraft designed to take off and land vertically using electrical power rather than by burning hydrocarbon fuels. One such aircraft, incorporating Syensqo's composite materials, was demonstrated at the Farnborough International Airshow in the UK in July 2026; proponents envisage such vehicles eventually operating as short-distance air taxis for the general public. Composite materials have been used in aerospace for decades, Heinz says, but new industrial demands are prompting researchers to reconsider what the materials can do and how they are made. “We’re seeing a revitalization and a re-emphasis of the science and technology of composites, enabling the future of flight,” he says. “That could be electrification, or making new aircraft that fly faster, or further.” Blended materials, blended expertise “As they are highly engineered forms of matter, composite materials are incredibly versatile,” says Jonathan Meegan, a research fellow at Syensqo. By carefully selecting the ingredients used to create composite materials, researchers can control their thermomechanical performance. They can also add extra functionality by modifying the composition of the composite material to tune energy-absorbing properties, as well as develop damage resistance and tolerance. Other characteristics that can be tweaked include electrical or thermal conductivity, electromagnetic shielding, vibration damping and resistance against lightning strikes. Achieving this range of properties requires expertise from traditionally distinct disciplines to work together in cycles of development and optimization. Formulation scientists select and test the polymers and fibres used in a particular product, creating interfaces between fibre and matrix that characterization specialists then study. In parallel, polymer scientists investigate how raw materials and different polymers interact to deliver properties such as stiffness, strength and toughness. They work closely with computational scientists and mechanical engineers, combining modelling and physical testing to understand how a composite behaves and to create digital representations of the material. In parallel, manufacturing engineers develop the equipment and processes needed to produce the composite at scale, while specialists analyse materials-testing data and feed the results back into formulation development. “The industry is increasingly dynamic, and becoming more blended in terms of the skillsets of its workers,” Meegan says. “We are evolving to the point where you don’t have engineers, you don’t have chemists. You have people who understand composite materials.” Manufacturing at a new scale The Climate Impulse aircraft's radome was manufactured using Double Diaphragm Forming technology at Syensqo's Composite Application Center in Heanor, UK.Credit: SyensqoOne of the main challenges lies not so much in designing composite materials but finding the best way to manufacture them. Producing composite components can be slower than stamping sheet metal or performing high-speed machining of bulk metals. At the same time, growing demand for composite materials is increasing pressure on manufacturers to develop technologies that enable rapid, safe, efficient and repeatable processing. Responding to these pressures, Syensqo is manipulating both the chemistry of its composite materials and the form of the materials themselves to increase the speed at which they can be safely and reliably processed. Syensqo’s Double Diaphragm Forming method, for example, enables more efficient processing by integrating the pre-forming and pressing steps involved in pre-preg-based parts manufacture into a single process, reducing manufacturing time and labour. The company’s FusePly technology addresses another challenge by preparing the surface of a cured composite so it can be physically and chemically bonded into a structure. The approach is intended to reduce assembly time and could reduce the need to reinforce some bonded joints with mechanical fasteners, potentially leading to further mass reductions in airframes. Emerging manufacturing technologies create their own materials science challenges. Robots can rapidly deposit the composite material needed to create a part, but increasing deposition speed requires researchers to understand how the material interacts with the process. “Without tuning the process-relevant characteristics of the material during the entire deposition process, you run the risk of significant amounts of machine downtime and failing to achieve the desired level of performance in the final cured composite material,” Meegan says. It is another example, he adds, of a complex problem that requires manufacturing specialists and materials scientists to work together to develop innovative solutions. The aviation industry's rigorous focus on safety means new materials and manufacturing approaches must prove themselves before they can be widely adopted. A safety-first approach can make any industry built around highly validated technologies understandably cautious about change.“Trying to get the industry to think differently when they know what works is very difficult,” Heinz says. “But as an industry, we have to think differently if we want to continue to scale technologies.” The challenge, then, is no longer simply to make a composite that is lighter or stronger than metal. Researchers must design materials whose chemistry, structure and processing work together — and that can meet aviation’s demanding performance and safety requirements at industrial scale. For the next generation of aircraft, solving that manufacturing challenge could prove just as important as developing the next high-performance material.
